title: Who pays for tariffs? Insights from recent research
gist: Sixteen months of post-"Liberation Day" research converges on US consumers and firms bearing roughly 90 percent or more of the 2025 tariff burden, with one study attributing all post-pandemic excess inflation to tariffs and another putting the CPI effect near 0.8 percentage points by early 2026. Clausing and Obstfeld argue the intermediate-input channel, lost scale economies, quality degradation, and legal chaos make the "optimal tariff" a mirage, and that removing tariffs is the fastest available fix for affordability.

themes.theme: Tariff incidence lands on US buyers

insights.claim: Multiple 2026 studies (Amiti et al., Fajgelbaum and Khandelwal, Gopinath and Neiman) imply US consumers and firms together bore about 90 percent of the 2025 US tariff burden, meaning foreign exporters absorbed only a thin slice.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Model tariffs as a domestic consumption tax on US margins and household budgets, not as revenue extracted from abroad — the hit shows up in US corporate COGS and CPI, not in foreign terms of trade.
insights.quote: all find a degree of pass-through that implies that US buyers of imports—US consumers and firms together—bore about 90 percent of the tariff burden in 2025
insights.locator: Amiti et al.

insights.claim: The 2018-19 US tariff episode produced near-complete pass-through to US buyers across study after study, establishing that the 2025 result is a repeat rather than a novel finding.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The historical base rate argues against any forecast in which foreign suppliers eat the next tariff round; default assumption for margin models should be full domestic incidence.
insights.quote: study after study of the 2018-19 US tariffs found that US buyers of imports suffered essentially the entire burden of the tariffs, with nearly complete pass-through shown in the data.
insights.locator: Still, study after study of the 2018-19

insights.claim: Minton, Ray, and Somale (2026) find tariff pass-through to US consumer prices is complete roughly seven months after implementation with 1-to-1 price effects, and attribute the entirety of post-pandemic excess inflation to tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: If tariffs explain all excess inflation, the disinflation path is a policy choice rather than a demand-cycle question — a tariff rollback would be a fast, large downside surprise to CPI and a rates-market catalyst.
insights.quote: The authors find that tariffs account for the entirety of post-pandemic excess inflation (relative to pre-pandemic inflation).
insights.locator: One recent study (Minton, Ray, and Somale 2026

insights.claim: Cavallo, Llamas, and Vasquez (2026) measure a cumulative tariff effect on the US CPI of about 0.8 percentage points by early 2026, with pass-through still incomplete six months after implementation.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete size for the tariff wedge in headline inflation and, because pass-through was still incomplete, implies more price increases were still in the pipeline as of early 2026.
insights.quote: with a cumulative effect on the consumer price index (CPI) of about 0.8 percentage points by early 2026
insights.locator: Another examination using earlier data

insights.claim: The eagerness of foreign governments to negotiate under US tariff threats is itself evidence that foreign exporters cannot costlessly redirect exports elsewhere, so tariffs do inflict real damage abroad even while US buyers pay most of the bill.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Negotiating capitulation by trading partners is not a signal that they are paying the tariff — read foreign concessions as evidence of export-market dependence, not of favorable US incidence.
insights.quote: If foreign export firms could easily redirect exports to other partners without cutting prices, their governments could simply ignore US tariff threats without much consequence.
insights.locator: The Trump administration (and previously the Trump campaign)

insights.claim: Legal and policy uncertainty makes firms absorb tariffs in margins first, because they avoid price increases they may later have to reverse — which delays but does not cancel consumer price effects.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Near-term corporate margin compression is the leading indicator; consumer price increases are the lagging one — watch gross margins before watching CPI for tariff transmission.
insights.quote: In the face of policy uncertainty, firms may be more willing to suffer reduced margins in the short run to avoid price increases that they might have to reverse later.
insights.locator: But tariffs take time to affect consumer prices

insights.claim: Survey evidence as of mid-2026 shows US firms are still planning price increases in response to tariffs imposed some time ago, meaning already-announced tariffs carry unrealized inflation still to come.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Inflation prints in late 2026 can rise from past tariffs alone with no new policy action — do not treat a tariff pause as an inflation peak.
insights.quote: firms are still planning price increases in response to tariffs that were imposed some time ago
insights.locator: They may pause price increases while lobbying

insights.claim: Scanner-level data from the 2018-19 China tariff episode (Bai, Jaccard, and Stumpner 2026) show full tariff pass-through coexisting with a product-replacement channel in which old barcodes were replaced by new products with higher price-per-weight ratios, i.e. shrinkflation.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Shelf-price indices understate true tariff pass-through because the effect hides in package size and product churn — standard CPI-based tariff estimates are biased low.
insights.quote: whereby old products were replaced by new products (with different bar codes) that had higher price/weight ratios ("shrinkflation")
insights.locator: Bai, Jaccard, and Stumpner (2026)

insights.claim: Tariffs have measurably degraded the quality of US imports (Ahn, Rotunno, and Ruta 2026), a firm-response mechanism that shows up as worse goods rather than as visible price increases.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Quality downgrading is an unmeasured welfare loss that also erodes brand and pricing power over time for import-reliant retailers and manufacturers.
insights.quote: It also finds that the quality of US imports has declined
insights.locator: Another recent study finds that US importers bear the full burden

insights.claim: Tariffs on imported inputs make US manufacturers pay more for components than their foreign competitors do, directly reducing US exporters' ability to compete in foreign markets.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Input-tariff exposure is a relative-cost disadvantage versus foreign peers — screen export-heavy US industrials for imported-input intensity, especially those without exemptions.
insights.quote: Tariffs reduce exporting firms' ability to compete in foreign markets, since US manufacturers must pay more for imported inputs than their competitors abroad.
insights.locator: Effect on intermediate business costs

insights.claim: The Trump administration has exempted some key firms and industries, including AI, from tariffs on inputs, while tariffs on steel and aluminum remain — creating a two-tier cost structure between exempted and unexempted manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Exemption status is a tradable dispersion factor: AI-adjacent hardware buyers get input relief while metals-consuming manufacturers absorb full cost — a long-exempt / short-exposed pairing.
insights.quote: Even the Trump administration recognizes this dynamic, which is why it has exempted some key firms and industries (including AI) from tariffs on inputs.
insights.locator: Even the Trump administration recognizes this dynamic

insights.claim: Blue collar employment in the US has been disappointing at best under the tariff regime, undercutting the claim that input tariffs rebuild manufacturing jobs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The political payoff the tariffs were sold on is not materializing in labor data, raising the odds of policy reversal or redesign ahead of electoral pressure.
insights.quote: the overall jobs picture for blue collar employment has been disappointing at best, as shown in the figure below
insights.locator: Yet other manufacturing firms are less lucky

insights.claim: JPMorganChase (2026) analysis finds midsize US firms may be bearing an especially significant cost from tariffs, a burden concentration distinct from large exempted firms and from small importers.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Credit and equity risk from tariffs is concentrated in the mid-cap tier that lacks both lobbying access and supplier-switching scale — a screen for private credit and middle-market lenders.
insights.quote: midsize firms may be bearing an especially significant cost from tariffs
insights.locator: The intermediate-input cost channel is also negative

insights.claim: Historical evidence assembled by den Besten et al. (2026) shows tariffs have tended to have contractionary macroeconomic effects throughout history, with the intermediate-input cost channel one reason why.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Treat tariffs as a supply-side contractionary shock — stagflationary for asset allocation rather than merely inflationary or merely protectionist.
insights.locator: one reason den Besten et al.

insights.claim: Stephen Miran's June 2026 claim that OBBBA's more generous investment deduction provisions offset higher tariff costs on imported inputs fails because firms still pay the after-tax cost of inputs — deductibility never makes a cost free.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Discount official arguments that tax provisions neutralize tariff costs — the margin hit to import-dependent firms is real regardless of expensing rules.
insights.quote: Indeed, Miran's logic implies that a $25 minimum wage wouldn't be a problem for firms either, since wage costs are deductible.
insights.locator: In June 2026, Stephen Miran

insights.claim: The higher deficits and debt generated by OBBBA imply higher interest rates that crowd out domestic investment, adding a second-order fiscal drag on top of the tariff cost channel.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The tax-side offset story cuts the other way for rates — long-end supply pressure compounds rather than cushions the tariff shock to capex.
insights.quote: Further, the higher deficits/debt from OBBBA imply higher interest rates, which crowd out domestic investment.
insights.locator: Further, the higher deficits/debt from OBBBA

themes.theme: Lost scale economies: burdens above 100 percent

insights.claim: Because tariffs shrink import order sizes and destroy scale economies, the combined burden on foreign exporters and US importers can total more than 100 percent of the tariff itself (Ganapati and Hottman 2026).
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariff cost models that split a fixed 100 percent between the two sides understate total economic damage — the deadweight loss is larger than the revenue raised.
insights.quote: both parties can together face burdens that total more than 100 percent of the size of the tariff, harming exporters and importers simultaneously due to the loss of scale economies
insights.locator: Forgone scale economies—which normally lower costs

insights.claim: Firms respond to tariffs by lobbying for exemptions and searching for cheaper foreign suppliers, activities the authors classify as additional real business costs of the tariff regime rather than adaptation gains.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Rent-seeking and supplier-search costs are an invisible tax on corporate management attention; firms with existing Washington access hold a structural advantage over rivals.
insights.quote: including lobbying for exemptions or for new tariffs on competitors
insights.locator: Conclusion

themes.theme: Legal fragility of the tariff regime

insights.claim: The Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful in February 2026, the US International Trade Court ruled the replacement Section 122 tariffs unlawful in May 2026 (under appeal), and the expanded use of Section 301 to recreate the IEEPA regime is also vulnerable to legal challenge.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The tariff regime rests on serially invalidated legal authorities — court dates are binary catalysts for import-exposed equities, refund claims, and inflation expectations.
insights.quote: The Supreme Court ruled the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) unlawful in February 2026
insights.locator: The Supreme Court ruled the tariffs imposed

insights.claim: To justify new tariffs on Canada the administration has invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff law, reaching for an obscure and historically discredited statutory authority.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Resort to a 1930-era provision signals the administration is running out of durable legal cover, raising the probability that Canada tariffs are unwound in court.
insights.quote: To justify new tariffs on Canada, the administration has invoked Section 338
insights.locator: To justify new tariffs on Canada

insights.claim: The authors argue removing tariffs is the fastest available policy answer to US affordability and grocery-price concerns, because housing, healthcare, and education costs require far slower structural reform.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Affordability politics create a real policy path to tariff rollback; the authors also flag that cutting tariffs on construction materials would be significant for the building industry.
insights.quote: If policymakers desire a quick and easy response to affordability concerns, removing the tariffs would be an obvious answer.
insights.locator: Thus, the preponderance of evidence indicates

insights.claim: Clausing and Obstfeld conclude the optimal tariff is a mirage with little practical relevance, and that the Trump tariff war simultaneously undermines the postwar trade system and demonstrates why that system was built.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing,Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The institutional case against tariffs is being restated by mainstream trade economists — expect continued policy pushback and elevated probability of eventual multilateral repair trades.
insights.quote: The "optimal tariff" is a mirage, useful as a classroom exercise but with little practical relevance.
insights.locator: Conclusion
